newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-rightist Le Pen claims growing strength.
newsitem.headline: French far-rightist Le Pen claims growing strength.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said on Monday his National Front party had grown in strength since his public espousal of racial inequality and vowed to keep up his offensive against the political mainstream.
"What are they going to do to me? Gas me? assassinate me? Machine-gun me? What can they do to force people to vote for the 'band of four'?" he asked in a television interview.
The four major parties, he said, criticised him to mask their own weakness.

In local by-election run-offs on Sunday, candidates from the governing centre-right edged out the Front with support from the Left in the southern city of Toulon and in Chaville in suburban Paris after the Front candidate led in first-round voting.

But the Front's scores were higher than in previous elections in those districts, and the Front candidate led the field after an initial round of voting on Sunday for a departmental council post in the Riviera capital Nice.
"This is a major victory," Le Pen, who scored 15 percent in last year's presidential elections, told France 2 television.

Le Pen, whose party's slogan is "France for the French", triggered a flood of protest this month with repeated remarks that racial inequality was "obvious" and "a fact", though he has denied that he is racist or antisemitic.
After his remarks, Prime Minister Alain Juppe called Le Pen "deeply, almost viscerally racist, antisemitic and xenophobic".
Le Pen, who last week had urged Juppe to resign, on Monday cranked up his rhetoric, calling the prime minister "a huckster, anti-national and a criminal against humanity".

Le Pen also had harsh criticism for a plan by Justice Minister Jacques Toubon to tighten French laws against inciting racial hatred, calling the proposal a "totalitarian law...that obviously targets the National Front".
Numerous politicians, rights groups and other civic leaders demanded that Le Pen be prosecuted over his statements on racial inequality.
But Toubon concluded the remarks fell through loopholes in the law, and on Friday he sent a draft bill to plug those loopholes to the National Consultative Human Rights Committee.
The bill is expected to go before the National Assembly within weeks.

Le Pen said the proposed legislation showed the government's "formidable weakness" due to its inability to solve the problems considered most important by the French people, which he identified as unemployment, immigration and insecurity.
"I intend in the days ahead to fight back, and to press the National Front's advantage," he said.
